That <reading>eat a duck</reading> moment, receiving with your head down, is <vocabulary form="頂く">to receive and eat, humbly</vocabulary>, said as <reading>いただく</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Mixed — 差（さ）on'yomi ＋ し ＋ 上（あ）kun'yomi ＋ げ ＋ る.
items.mnemonic_text: Offering something up respectfully: sashiageru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Noticing the <kanji form="差">difference</kanji> in rank between you and the higher-ranked person, you raise the gift <kanji form="上">up</kanji> with both arms so it travels toward them. Handing something upward across that gap is to <vocabulary form="差し上げる">give, humbly</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 下（くだ）＋さる.
items.mnemonic_text: Graciously handing something down: kudasaru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: An honored person hands the gift <kanji form="下">down</kanji> to where you stand, well <kanji form="下">below</kanji> their seat. A present that travels downward from someone that far over you is one they <vocabulary form="下さる">give you, honorifically</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kaa, the fire-breathing crow, perches on the power line and drops little glowing medals of <reading>kudos</reading> onto everyone waiting below. A gift handed down from a bird perched that high is <vocabulary form="下さる">to give, honorifically</vocabulary>, landing with the sound <reading>くださる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 承（しょう）＋知（ち）＋する, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: Receiving (承) knowledge (知) humbly: shouchi suru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: An order comes in and lands dead center, the way the arrow thumps into the target: now you <kanji form="知">know</kanji> it. Bowing to show it struck home and you will carry it out is how you <vocabulary form="承知する">acknowledge an instruction, humbly</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 話（はな）＋せる.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of hanasu: able to speak.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Hand the nonstop <kanji form="話">talker</kanji> with the wagging tongue an open microphone and the words just pour out, no gap anywhere. Being able to let language run like that is what it means to <vocabulary form="話せる">be able to speak</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 話 is read 「はな」 from 話す, so <vocabulary form="話せる">can speak</vocabulary> comes out as <reading>はなせる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 書（か）＋ける.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of kaku: able to write.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="書">write</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="書ける">can write</vocabulary> word are the same character, so they mean the same thing. The added ending only shifts it from doing the writing to being able to do it.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 書 is read 「か」 from 書く, so <vocabulary form="書ける">can write</vocabulary> comes out as <reading>かける</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 読（よ）＋める.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of yomu: able to read.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="読">read</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="読める">can read</vocabulary> word are the same character, so they point at the same meaning. The extra ending just moves it from reading to being able to read.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 読 is read 「よ」 from 読む, so <vocabulary form="読める">can read</vocabulary> comes out as <reading>よめる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 使（つか）＋える.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of tsukau: usable.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Nothing new happens here: the <kanji form="使">use</kanji> kanji you already know is exactly what <vocabulary form="使える">can use</vocabulary> means.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already met 「つか」 in 使う, so <vocabulary form="使える">can use</vocabulary> just wears that same reading with a new tail: <reading>つかえる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 行（い）＋ける.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of iku: able to go.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="行">go</kanji> kanji stands on its own here, so <vocabulary form="行ける">can go</vocabulary> is that same kanji and not one idea more.
items.reading_mnemonic: The 「い」 in this word is the one from 行く that you already know, so <vocabulary form="行ける">can go</vocabulary> comes out as <reading>いける</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 来（こ）＋られる.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of kuru: able to come.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="来">come</kanji> kanji is the whole of this word, so <vocabulary form="来られる">can come</vocabulary> holds nothing the character did not already carry.
items.reading_mnemonic: Once the runaway goat is <reading>collared</reading> and leashed, it <vocabulary form="来られる">can come</vocabulary> to you from right across the field. A goat you can call back in like that is <reading>こられる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 食（た）＋べられる.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of taberu: able to eat.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="食">eat</kanji> kanji does all the work on its own here, so <vocabulary form="食べられる">can eat</vocabulary> means just what that character has always meant.
items.reading_mnemonic: That 「た」 is the same one 食べる taught you earlier, so <vocabulary form="食べられる">can eat</vocabulary> is simply <reading>たべられる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 飲（の）＋める.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of nomu: able to drink.
items.meaning_mnemonic: No story to build here: the <kanji form="飲">drink</kanji> kanji is the whole word, and <vocabulary form="飲める">can drink</vocabulary> means the very same thing.
items.reading_mnemonic: You know 「の」 already from 飲む, so <vocabulary form="飲める">can drink</vocabulary> follows straight on as <reading>のめる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 見（み）＋られる.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of miru: able to see.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="見">see</kanji> kanji does not change when it becomes a word, so <vocabulary form="見られる">can see</vocabulary> is simply the character you have already met.
items.reading_mnemonic: This 「み」 is the reading you picked up in 見る, so <vocabulary form="見られる">can see</vocabulary> comes out as <reading>みられる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 出（で）＋来（き）＋る.
items.mnemonic_text: Kanji form of dekiru: to be possible.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Once every part has <kanji form="来">come</kanji> in, a finished thing <kanji form="出">exits</kanji> the far end of the line. That finished thing is proof the whole job was <vocabulary form="出来る">possible</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 泳（およ）＋げる.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of oyogu: able to swim.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Step off the riverbank into deep water and you do not go under; your limbs already know the strokes. Holding yourself up and moving through the water on your own is what it means that you <vocabulary form="泳げる">can swim</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 「およ」 from 泳ぐ, so <vocabulary form="泳げる">can swim</vocabulary> simply becomes <reading>およげる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 走（はし）＋れる.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of hashiru: able to run.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Same character, same meaning: the <kanji form="走">run</kanji> kanji you already know is all there is to <vocabulary form="走れる">can run</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The 「はし」 here is the same one from 走る, so <vocabulary form="走れる">can run</vocabulary> reads as <reading>はしれる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 会（あ）＋える.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of au: able to meet.
items.meaning_mnemonic: There is nothing extra to learn here, since the <kanji form="会">meet</kanji> kanji and the word <vocabulary form="会える">can meet</vocabulary> point at exactly the same idea.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already say 「あ」 this way in 会う, so <vocabulary form="会える">can meet</vocabulary> is nothing more than <reading>あえる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 買（か）＋える.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of kau: able to buy.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="買">buy</kanji> kanji carries straight over into this word, so <vocabulary form="買える">can buy</vocabulary> holds no meaning the kanji did not already.
items.reading_mnemonic: That 「か」 is the reading 買う already gave you, so <vocabulary form="買える">can buy</vocabulary> lands as <reading>かえる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 乗（の）＋れる.
items.mnemonic_text: The potential form of noru: able to ride.
items.meaning_mnemonic: This word adds nothing to its kanji: <vocabulary form="乗れる">can ride</vocabulary> is the <kanji form="乗">ride</kanji> kanji you have already met, unchanged.
items.reading_mnemonic: The 「の」 in this word comes straight from 乗る, so <vocabulary form="乗れる">can ride</vocabulary> simply becomes <reading>のれる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 行（い）＋かせる.
items.mnemonic_text: The causative of iku: making someone go.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At its core this word is still the <kanji form="行">go</kanji> kanji. The tail added on means you <vocabulary form="行かせる">make or let someone go</vocabulary>, whether they want to or not.
items.reading_mnemonic: Same 「い」 as in 行く, so <vocabulary form="行かせる">to make/let go</vocabulary> keeps that opening sound and becomes <reading>いかせる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 食（た）＋べさせる.
items.mnemonic_text: The causative of taberu: making someone eat.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Underneath, this is only the <kanji form="食">eat</kanji> kanji again. The extra endings shift it to mean you <vocabulary form="食べさせる">make or let another person eat</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The 「た」 is the one 食べる gave you, so <vocabulary form="食べさせる">to make/let eat</vocabulary> starts the same and runs on to <reading>たべさせる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: The causative of yaru: making someone do it.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Run a <reading>yard sale</reading> and you get one afternoon to <vocabulary form="やらせる">make or let someone else do</vocabulary> every bit of the lifting and pricing. Handing the whole driveway to other hands like that is <reading>やらせる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 待（ま）＋たされる.
items.mnemonic_text: The causative-passive of matsu: being kept waiting.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="待">wait</kanji> kanji sits at the centre of this word unchanged. The endings stacked after it turn plain waiting into <vocabulary form="待たされる">being made to wait</vocabulary> by someone who will not hurry.
items.reading_mnemonic: You learned 「ま」 back in 待つ, so the drawn-out <vocabulary form="待たされる">to be made to wait</vocabulary> is still just <reading>またされる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 叱（しか）＋られる.
items.mnemonic_text: The passive of shikaru: on the receiving end of a scolding.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Knock a jar off Grandma Kane's shelf and every cat goes still while she turns and scolds you in a long, rising voice. Standing there and taking all of it is what it means <vocabulary form="叱られる">to be scolded</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 「しか」 from 叱る, so the version done to you, <vocabulary form="叱られる">to be scolded</vocabulary>, is <reading>しかられる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 褒（ほ）＋められる.
items.mnemonic_text: The passive of homeru: receiving praise.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Hand a drawing to the teacher and she holds it up to the whole class, naming every good line in it. Having your work lifted up for the whole room to see is what it means <vocabulary form="褒められる">to be praised</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 「ほ」 from 褒める, so the same thing coming back at you, <vocabulary form="褒められる">to be praised</vocabulary>, is <reading>ほめられる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 泣（な）＋かれる.
items.mnemonic_text: The passive of naku: suffering from someone's crying.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The person beside you suddenly bursts out <kanji form="泣">crying</kanji>, and now their misery is your problem to deal with. Being left holding someone else's tears like that is being <vocabulary form="泣かれる">cried at</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 「な」 from 泣く, so that same crying aimed at you, <vocabulary form="泣かれる">to be cried at (adversity)</vocabulary>, is <reading>なかれる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 殺（ころ）＋す.
items.mnemonic_text: A blow (殳) striking down: to kill.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Yank the wrong lever on the old mower and the motor goes quiet for good under your hands. Ending a running thing on purpose like that is what it means <vocabulary form="殺す">to kill</vocabulary> it.
items.reading_mnemonic: The frog <reading>chorus</reading> at the riverbank drones so flat and so long that it could <vocabulary form="殺す">kill</vocabulary> every houseplant on the windowsill. A sound that deadly is <reading>ころす</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 殺（ころ）＋される.
items.mnemonic_text: The passive of korosu: to be killed.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A beetle wanders onto the train track at exactly the wrong second. The 8:15 does not slow down, and being the one it happens to is <vocabulary form="殺される">to be killed</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 殺 is 「ころ」 from 殺す, the verb you first met it in, so <vocabulary form="殺される">to be killed</vocabulary> is <reading>ころされる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 出（で）＋かける.
items.mnemonic_text: Exiting (出) and setting off: dekakeru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Climbing out over the box rim is only the <kanji form="出">exit</kanji>. Once your feet hit the road and you keep walking, that is <vocabulary form="出かける">to go out / head out</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 出 is 「で」 from 出る, the verb it first showed up in, so <vocabulary form="出かける">to go out / head out</vocabulary> is <reading>でかける</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 取（と）＋り＋替（か）＋える.
items.mnemonic_text: Taking (取り) and changing (替える): to swap.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji form="取">take</kanji> the worn part out by the ear, the rude fast way, and drop a fresh one into the gap it left. Swapping the old for the new like that is <vocabulary form="取り替える">to exchange / replace</vocabulary>.

items.word_type: godan verb, transitive verb, intransitive verb
items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 繰（く）＋り＋返（かえ）＋す.
items.mnemonic_text: Reeling (繰り) something back (返す): to repeat.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You set the reel <kanji form="繰">winding</kanji> forward, it <kanji form="返">return</kanji>s to the very same mark, and your hand starts it winding again. Motion that keeps coming back to its start is <vocabulary form="繰り返す">to repeat</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 取（と）＋り＋掛（か）＋かる.
items.mnemonic_text: Taking (取り) hold (掛かる) of a task: to begin work.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You get a grip on the job and <kanji form="掛">hang</kanji> your whole weight from it, the rude fast way you would <kanji form="取">take</kanji> hold of someone by the ear. Latching on and leaning in like that is <vocabulary form="取り掛かる">to set about (a task)</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 持（も）＋ち＋帰（かえ）＋る.
items.mnemonic_text: Holding (持ち) and returning (帰る): to take away.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji form="持">hold</kanji> on the warm food box never loosens the whole walk home, right up to the moment you <kanji form="帰">return</kanji> through your own door. Carrying your meal back that way is <vocabulary form="持ち帰る">to take home / take out</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 連（つ）＋れて＋行（い）＋く.
items.mnemonic_text: Bringing (連れて) someone along as you go (行く).
items.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji form="行">go</kanji> off down the crossroads with your little brother gripped by the sleeve so he cannot peel away. Setting out with a person fastened to your side like that is <vocabulary form="連れて行く">to take (a person) along</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 連（つ）＋れて＋来（く）＋る.
items.mnemonic_text: Bringing (連れて) someone as you come (来る).
items.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji form="連">lead</kanji> a nervous friend up the path by the hand as the two of you <kanji form="来">come</kanji> toward the house. Turning up with an extra person beside you is <vocabulary form="連れて来る">to bring (a person)</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 持（も）＋って＋来（く）＋る.
items.mnemonic_text: Holding (持って) something as you come (来る).
items.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji form="持">hold</kanji> stays locked around the umbrella as you <kanji form="来">come</kanji> back in through the door. Arriving with the thing still in your hand is <vocabulary form="持って来る">to bring (a thing)</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 持（も）＋って＋行（い）＋く.
items.mnemonic_text: Holding (持って) something as you go (行く).
items.meaning_mnemonic: You clamp your <kanji form="持">hold</kanji> around the lunchbox and <kanji form="行">go</kanji> straight out through the crossroads with it. Carrying the thing away from the house is <vocabulary form="持って行く">to take (a thing)</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 話（はな）＋し＋合（あ）＋う.
items.mnemonic_text: Talking (話し) together (合う): to discuss.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Each side <kanji form="話">talk</kanji>s, story after story, until the two accounts finally <kanji form="合">fit</kanji> together. Talk that both sides work at until it matches is <vocabulary form="話し合う">to discuss / talk over</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 見（み）＋送（おく）＋る.
items.mnemonic_text: Watching (見) someone off (送る): to see off.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You keep your <kanji form="見">see</kanji>ing eye locked on your friend while the platform <kanji form="送">send</kanji>s her off down a track you may not follow. Watching a person go until she is out of sight is <vocabulary form="見送る">to see off</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 見（み）＋回（まわ）＋す.
items.mnemonic_text: Turning (回す) one's view (見): to look around.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji form="見">see</kanji>ing eye travels one full <kanji form="回">round</kanji> of the room, past every wall and back to where it started. Sweeping your gaze in a circle like that is <vocabulary form="見回す">to look around</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 見（み）＋つけ＋出（だ）＋す.
items.mnemonic_text: Finding (見つけ) something and drawing it out (出す).
items.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji form="見">see</kanji>ing eye catches the hidden thing, and you haul it up over the box rim until it <kanji form="出">exit</kanji>s into daylight. Dragging a buried fact into the open is <vocabulary form="見つけ出す">to discover / find out</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 考（かんが）＋え＋出（だ）＋す.
items.mnemonic_text: Thinking (考え) something into being (出す): to devise.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji form="考">think</kanji>, tracing one old thought down its kinked track until a new idea works loose. Forcing that idea to <kanji form="出">exit</kanji> into the open is <vocabulary form="考え出す">to think up / devise</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — やり＋直（なお）＋す.
items.mnemonic_text: Doing (やり) it fixed again (直す): to redo.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The moment the work goes wrong, you <kanji form="直">straightaway</kanji> tear it down and carry the pieces back to step one. Building it again from the start like that is <vocabulary form="やり直す">to redo / start over</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 直 is 「なお」 from 直す, the verb it first appeared in, so <vocabulary form="やり直す">to redo / start over</vocabulary> is <reading>やりなおす</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Doing a favor and giving it: yatte ageru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Out on the <reading>yacht, a giraffe</reading> leans up and knots the top sail no sailor can reach, doing it for the whole crew. Doing the work so that someone else gains is <vocabulary form="やってあげる">to do (for someone)</vocabulary>, the outward giving inside <reading>やってあげる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Someone doing a favor for me: yatte kureru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Back on the <reading>yacht, a crew</reading> of borrowed hands bails the flooded hull while you only hold the tiller. Someone else doing the work for you, while you sit back, is <vocabulary form="やってくれる">to do (for me)</vocabulary>, the inward favour inside <reading>やってくれる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Receiving the favor of an action: yatte morau.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Off the <reading>yacht, a moray</reading> eel is the only thing that will chew the fouled anchor rope free, so down it goes to do the job. Getting someone else to do the work in your place is <vocabulary form="やってもらう">to have (someone) do</vocabulary>, the sound sitting inside <reading>やってもらう</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 作（つく）＋ってあげる.
items.mnemonic_text: Making something and giving it: tsukutte ageru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="作">make</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="作ってあげる">to make (for someone)</vocabulary> word are the same word, so at heart it just means make. The tail on the end only adds that you make the thing for someone else, not for yourself.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 作 is 「つく」 from 作る, the verb it first appeared in, so <vocabulary form="作ってあげる">to make (for someone)</vocabulary> is <reading>つくってあげる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 見（み）＋せてくれる.
items.mnemonic_text: Someone showing something to me: misete kureru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A friend makes you <kanji form="見">see</kanji> something by holding it up in front of your face. That small favour, done for you, is to <vocabulary form="見せてくれる">show (to me)</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 見 is 「み」 from 見る, the verb to look, so <vocabulary form="見せてくれる">to show (to me)</vocabulary> is <reading>みせてくれる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 教（おし）＋えてもらう.
items.mnemonic_text: Receiving the favor of being taught: oshiete morau.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="教">teach</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="教えてもらう">to have (someone) teach</vocabulary> word are the same word, so they carry the same meaning.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 教 is 「おし」 from 教える, the verb to teach, so <vocabulary form="教えてもらう">to have (someone) teach</vocabulary> is <reading>おしえてもらう</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 書（か）＋いてあげる.
items.mnemonic_text: Writing something and giving it: kaite ageru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="書">write</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="書いてあげる">to write (for someone)</vocabulary> word are one and the same, so the meaning does not change.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 書 is 「か」 from 書く, the verb to write, so <vocabulary form="書いてあげる">to write (for someone)</vocabulary> is <reading>かいてあげる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 手（て）＋伝（つだ）＋ってくれる.
items.mnemonic_text: Someone lending a hand for me: tetsudatte kureru.
items.furigana: 手伝[てつだ]ってくれる
items.meaning_mnemonic: Someone puts a <kanji form="手">hand</kanji> to your job and lets their own plans <kanji form="伝">go along</kanji> with your work instead. Doing that for you is to <vocabulary form="手伝ってくれる">help (me)</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 貸（か）＋してもらう.
items.mnemonic_text: Receiving the favor of a loan: kashite morau.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You ask, and the owner agrees to <kanji form="貸">lend</kanji> you the thing you need. Walking off with it on that promise is to <vocabulary form="貸してもらう">have (something) lent</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 貸 is 「か」 from 貸す, the verb to lend, so <vocabulary form="貸してもらう">to have (something) lent</vocabulary> is <reading>かしてもらう</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 送（おく）＋ってあげる.
items.mnemonic_text: Sending something as a favor: okutte ageru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="送">send</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="送ってあげる">to send (for someone)</vocabulary> word are the same character, so they mean the same thing.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 送 is 「おく」 from 送る, the verb to send, so <vocabulary form="送ってあげる">to send (for someone)</vocabulary> is <reading>おくってあげる</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 虫（むし）.
items.mnemonic_text: A curling little bug: mushi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Tip up the old flowerpot by the back step and the packed soil under it comes alive with tiny legs and feelers that pour away from the daylight. Every scurrying speck down there is an <vocabulary form="虫">insect / bug</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Leave a peach on Koichi's counter until it turns <reading>mushy</reading>, and by morning the soft brown patch is crawling with every kind of <vocabulary form="虫">insect / bug</vocabulary>. Koichi flicks them off and mutters 「<reading>むし</reading>」.

items.reading_composition: On'yomi — 蝶（ちょう）.
items.mnemonic_text: Insect (虫) with delicate wings: a butterfly.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A scrap of coloured paper lifts off the shrine path and flutters between the mossy steps, folding shut and opening again as it climbs the air. That drifting pair of painted wings is a <vocabulary form="蝶">butterfly</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 猿（さる）.
items.mnemonic_text: A dog-like beast (犭) still (袁): a monkey.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A grey shape drops onto the trailhead vending machine, pops the flap with quick clever fingers and swings back up a pine with a stolen can. Only a <vocabulary form="猿">monkey</vocabulary> robs a machine like that.
items.reading_mnemonic: Down at the riverbank a <vocabulary form="猿">monkey</vocabulary> snatches <reading>a sarong</reading> off the drying line and wears it up a tree. The washer-woman shakes her fist and yells 「<reading>さる</reading>」.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 馬（うま）.
items.mnemonic_text: A galloping horse with a flowing mane: uma.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The animal that walks over to the paddock fence stands taller than you at the shoulder, long-faced, with a mane down its neck and a sweeping tail. That shape and size is a <vocabulary form="馬">horse</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A toddler on the trail points at the animal being led past and gasps <reading>ooh, ma</reading> at her mother. The thing she means is a <vocabulary form="馬">horse</vocabulary>, and the word she wants is 「<reading>うま</reading>」.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 牛（うし）.
items.mnemonic_text: Horns over a body: a cow.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="牛">cow</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="牛">cow</vocabulary> word are exactly the same character, so they mean the same thing.
items.reading_mnemonic: The dairy farmer leans on the gate watching his best milker chew and sighs that <reading>ooh, she</reading> is a fine one. The animal he means is a <vocabulary form="牛">cow</vocabulary>, and he calls her 「<reading>うし</reading>」.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 豚（ぶた）.
items.mnemonic_text: Flesh (月) matched with a boar's (豕) body: a pig.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Behind Koichi's konbini the scraps bin lies tipped over, and a fat pink animal stands in the spill with its snout down, grunting as it eats. Nothing empties a bin like a <vocabulary form="豚">pig</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The farmer fattens the animal every night on a bucket of <reading>butter</reading> and kitchen scraps until it can barely walk. That round, greasy thing is a <vocabulary form="豚">pig</vocabulary>, and he calls it 「<reading>ぶた</reading>」.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 羊（ひつじ）.
items.mnemonic_text: A woolly head with curling horns: a sheep.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="羊">sheep</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="羊">sheep</vocabulary> word are the same character, so they point at the same animal.
items.reading_mnemonic: The shepherd sends her dog with one command, <reading>hit, Suzy</reading>, and it circles the woolly flock and drives them through the gate. Each fat woolly one is a <vocabulary form="羊">sheep</vocabulary>, called 「<reading>ひつじ</reading>」.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 狐（きつね）.
items.mnemonic_text: A dog-like beast (犭) melon-shaped (瓜) tail: a fox.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At dusk a low red-brown shape slips along the treeline by the school field, quick and quiet, a white-tipped tail held straight out behind. That build and that tail mean a <vocabulary form="狐">fox</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The raider picks the coop latch every night and leaves it closed so tidily the farmer blames himself. <reading>Kit, so neat</reading> a thief has to be a <vocabulary form="狐">fox</vocabulary>, and the word is 「<reading>きつね</reading>」.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 熊（くま）.
items.mnemonic_text: A powerful beast standing over fire-like paws: a bear.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The beekeeper finds three hives smashed flat, the honey frames licked clean and claw marks gouged deep in the wood. Only a <vocabulary form="熊">bear</vocabulary> robs hives like that.
items.reading_mnemonic: Curled asleep in the hollow log, the animal is a perfect furry <reading>comma</reading>, nose tucked to tail. Nudge that 「<reading>くま</reading>」 awake and it unrolls into a very large <vocabulary form="熊">bear</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: On'yomi — 象（ぞう）.
items.mnemonic_text: A long-trunked beast shape: an elephant.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Behind the zoo fence stands a grey animal the size of a truck, its legs like pillars and its nose long enough to pick a bun off the ground. That reaching nose alone means <vocabulary form="象">elephant</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 蛇（へび）.
items.mnemonic_text: Insect (虫) shape twisting like an earth-snake (它): a snake.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The hose coiled on the riverbank path lifts one end, flicks a thin forked tongue, and pours itself smoothly off into the long grass. A rope that moves on its own is a <vocabulary form="蛇">snake</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A hiker nudges what looks like a <reading>heavy</reading> length of rope lying across the trail, and it coils back on itself and hisses. Rope that fights back is a <vocabulary form="蛇">snake</vocabulary>, 「<reading>へび</reading>」.

items.reading_composition: Irregular — くも cannot be assembled from the dictionary readings of 蜘蛛.
items.mnemonic_text: Two insect (虫) characters weaving a web: a spider.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You step off the porch at dawn and walk face-first through a wide sticky net strung across the doorway. Sitting dead centre with its legs spread is the <vocabulary form="蜘蛛">spider</vocabulary> that spun it overnight.
items.reading_mnemonic: Mo walks the mountain trail into the same face-height web every dawn and yells <reading>come, Mo</reading> at nobody. The weaver that keeps rebuilding it is a <vocabulary form="蜘蛛">spider</vocabulary>, 「<reading>くも</reading>」.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 蚊（か）.
items.mnemonic_text: Insect (虫) that hums like the number ten crossed: a mosquito.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The high thin whine circles your ear in the dark, stops, and a second later a hot itch rises on your arm. The thing that bit you and left that whine is a <vocabulary form="蚊">mosquito</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: <reading>Kaa</reading> the crow snaps at the whining speck by the power line, breathes one puff of flame, and swallows it charred. What she just ate was a <vocabulary form="蚊">mosquito</vocabulary>, and her caw after is 「<reading>か</reading>」.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 蝿（はえ）.
items.mnemonic_text: Insect (虫) buzzing around: a fly.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You set the bowl down for one minute and three of them already crowd the rim, rubbing their legs and testing the food. Nothing finds a meal faster than a <vocabulary form="蝿">fly (insect)</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The farmhand forks over the <reading>hay</reading> pile and a grey cloud lifts off it buzzing, then drops straight back down. Every dot in that cloud is a <vocabulary form="蝿">fly (insect)</vocabulary>, 「<reading>はえ</reading>」.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 自（し）＋然（ぜん）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: One's own (自) natural state (然): nature.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Anything that is the way it is by its own <kanji form="自">self</kanji>, just that <kanji form="然">sort of thing</kanji> with nobody shaping it, is <vocabulary form="自然">nature</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 太（たい）＋陽（よう）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: The great (太) yang (陽): the sun.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The sky's one genuinely <kanji form="太">fat</kanji> light is too bright to look straight at, and every shadow on the ground points away from it. That light is the <vocabulary form="太陽">sun (formal)</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 星（ほし）＋空（ぞら）. Rendaku: 空 そら → ぞら.
items.mnemonic_text: Stars (星) filling the sky (空): a starry sky.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Wait until a <kanji form="空">sky</kanji> that looked empty all day fills after dark with thousands of small points of light, and you are looking at a <vocabulary form="星空">starry sky</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 波（なみ）.
items.mnemonic_text: Water (氵) taking on skin-like (皮) ripples: a wave.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Out on the open sea the water never settles; it stacks itself into a moving ridge, throws that ridge at the land, then draws back to build the next. Each moving ridge is a <vocabulary form="波">wave</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Nami the lifeguard names every <vocabulary form="波">wave</vocabulary> after herself. She stands on her tower shouting <reading>なみ</reading> at each wall of water as it rolls in, and the sound <reading>Nami</reading> has meant wave on that beach ever since.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 森（もり）.
items.mnemonic_text: Three trees (木) together: a forest.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The single character <kanji>forest</kanji> is the entire word, nothing added and nothing dropped. What you met as a kanji and what you say out loud as <vocabulary>forest</vocabulary> are the same thing.
items.reading_mnemonic: Walk into the <vocabulary>forest</vocabulary> and a mole named <reading>Morrie</reading> shoves his head up between two roots. He insists <reading>もり</reading> is his family name, since he dug every tunnel under these trees.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 林（はやし）.
items.mnemonic_text: Two trees (木) together: a small wood.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="林">grove</kanji> kanji you have already met and the <vocabulary form="林">woods / grove</vocabulary> word are the same character, so they carry the same meaning.
items.reading_mnemonic: A forest ranger named <reading>Hayashi</reading> has replanted the same <vocabulary form="林">woods / grove</vocabulary> three times after three separate fires. The locals gave up on the map name and just call the trees <reading>はやし</reading> after him.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 池（いけ）.
items.mnemonic_text: Water (氵) pooling beside a snake-like (也) shape: a pond.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="池">pond</kanji> kanji and the <vocabulary form="池">pond</vocabulary> word are the same character, so of course they mean exactly the same thing.
items.reading_mnemonic: The <vocabulary form="池">pond</vocabulary> behind Grandma Kane's shrine turns green and <reading>icky</reading> every August, thick enough to float a fallen leaf on top. The cats pick their way around it and she just calls it <reading>いけ</reading> and tops it up.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 岩（いわ）.
items.mnemonic_text: A mountain (山) of stone (石): a boulder.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A single stone in the field is too big to lift, too heavy to roll, and was sitting there before the farm was. A stone that large and that settled is a <vocabulary form="岩">rock / boulder</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A hiker on the mountain trail swears the biggest <vocabulary form="岩">rock / boulder</vocabulary> up there is shaped exactly like the state of <reading>Iowa</reading>. Everyone else just calls it <reading>いわ</reading> and keeps climbing.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 砂（すな）.
items.mnemonic_text: Stone (石) broken into few (少) grains: sand.
items.meaning_mnemonic: <vocabulary form="砂">Sand</vocabulary> is what a cliff turns into after the sea grinds at it for a few thousand years. What is left is a pile of grains so small they run through your fingers and still will not brush off.
items.reading_mnemonic: A cat drags a whole <reading>tuna</reading> onto the beach and pats it down under the <vocabulary form="砂">sand</vocabulary> to save for later. By evening it has forgotten which stretch of <reading>すな</reading> holds the fish.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 泥（どろ）.
items.mnemonic_text: Water (氵) mixed with soil, given a moon-shape twist: mud.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Mix plain dirt with enough rain and you get <vocabulary form="泥">mud</vocabulary>, a brown paste thick enough to hold a footprint and sticky enough to pull a boot off the foot that made it.
items.reading_mnemonic: Doro the farmhand goes to fetch water and comes back wearing half the riverbank, brown to the elbows with <vocabulary form="泥">mud</vocabulary>. Now one look at anyone in that state and the village just sighs <reading>どろ</reading>, said exactly like <reading>Doro</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 煙（けむり）.
items.mnemonic_text: Fire (火) rising through the west (西) sky: smoke.
items.meaning_mnemonic: When something burns, part of it leaves as a grey cloud that climbs, spreads flat under the ceiling, and stings your eyes. That rising grey cloud off a fire is <vocabulary form="煙">smoke</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The cook who trips the alarm most days insists the <vocabulary form="煙">smoke</vocabulary> is just him working from <reading>memory</reading>. The fire crew now radio <reading>けむり</reading> before he has even lit the stove.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 炎（ほのお）.
items.mnemonic_text: Two fires (火火) stacked: a flame.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Strike a match and a small pointed shape of light stands up on the tip, orange at the edges and bluish at the base. That upright, leaning tongue of burning light is a <vocabulary form="炎">flame</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A knight promises to guard the temple <vocabulary form="炎">flame</vocabulary> with his <reading>honor</reading> and never let it die. He falls asleep, it dies, and the other knights have whispered <reading>ほのお</reading> at him ever since.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 氷（こおり）.
items.mnemonic_text: Water (水) with a frozen edge: ice.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Water held cold enough for long enough stops behaving like a liquid and turns hard, clear and slippery. Water in that solid state is <vocabulary form="氷">ice</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: An old ice-cutter shows visitors where his crew once sawed winter <vocabulary form="氷">ice</vocabulary> from the lake in blocks, working it like a stone <reading>quarry</reading>. He still calls that frozen lake <reading>こおり</reading>, the word his crew used for the place.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 嵐（あらし）.
items.mnemonic_text: A mountain (山) wind (風): a storm.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Sometimes the wind, the rain, the black cloud and the noise all arrive together and stay for a whole day. A whole sky misbehaving at once is a <vocabulary form="嵐">storm</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A dock hand shouts <reading>a rush</reading> whenever the wind turns, and the crews haul every boat in. Nine times it is nothing, but the tenth is a real <vocabulary form="嵐">storm</vocabulary>, so the port still jumps at the shout, now worn down to <reading>あらし</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 台（たい）＋風（ふう）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: A platform (台) wind (風): a typhoon.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Give one <kanji form="風">wind</kanji> a name, a number, and its own <kanji form="台">pedestal</kanji> on every weather map, and that single most-watched storm is a <vocabulary form="台風">typhoon</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 地（じ）＋震（しん）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: The ground (地) trembling (震): an earthquake.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="地">ground</kanji> is the one thing built to stay still, so when it starts to <kanji form="震">shake</kanji> hard enough to knock cups off the shelf, you have an <vocabulary form="地震">earthquake</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 和（わ）＋風（ふう）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: Harmony's (和) style (風): Japanese-style.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You already know <kanji form="和">harmony</kanji> also stands for Japan itself, and <kanji form="風">wind</kanji> can mean the air or manner of a thing. So the Japanese manner of doing something is <vocabulary form="和風">Japanese-style</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 洋（よう）＋食（しょく）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: Ocean-crossed (洋) food (食): Western cuisine.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="洋">ocean</kanji> here carries its other sense, foreign. So <kanji form="食">food</kanji> that came from across the water, the fried and buttery knife-and-fork kind, is <vocabulary form="洋食">Western food</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 和（わ）＋食（しょく）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: Harmony's (和) food (食): Japanese cuisine.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Take that same <kanji form="和">harmony</kanji> that also stands for Japan, set it in front of <kanji form="食">food</kanji>, and you have the home-side cooking of rice, fish and miso that is <vocabulary form="和食">Japanese food</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 中（ちゅう）＋華（か）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: Middle (中) flower (華): Chinese style.
items.meaning_mnemonic: China's own name for itself sets the country at the <kanji form="中">middle</kanji> of the world and calls the culture there its <kanji form="華">splendor</kanji>. On a Japanese menu, <vocabulary form="中華">Chinese (cuisine)</vocabulary> is food from that middle kingdom.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Borrowed word: menyuu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A waiter at a packed diner is asked for the list of dishes by <reading>many ewe</reading> at the same moment, a whole coach tour of sheep. He keeps shouting that the <vocabulary form="メニュー">menu</vocabulary> is printed on the back of the placemat, and the sheep just bleat <reading>メニュー</reading> louder.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 注（ちゅう）＋文（もん）＋する, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: Pouring (注) a written request (文): to order.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You speak one clean <kanji form="文">sentence</kanji> across the counter, and a few minutes later a cup is <kanji form="注">poured</kanji> for you. Doing that on purpose is <vocabulary form="注文する">to order (food)</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 甘（あま）＋み.
items.mnemonic_text: The quality (み) of sweet (甘): sweetness.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The flavour children chase and dentists warn against, the one that makes you shut your eyes at the first bite of warm cake, is <vocabulary form="甘み">sweetness</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 甘 is 「あま」 from 甘い, so the noun for that flavour, <vocabulary form="甘み">sweetness</vocabulary>, is just <reading>あまみ</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: A sharp salty bite: shoppai.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Bite into a <reading>shop pie</reading> from the konbini and the filling is pure seawater. That sting is <reading>しょっぱい</reading>, painfully <vocabulary form="しょっぱい">salty</vocabulary>, and the い ending marks it as a describing word.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 苦（にが）＋い.
items.mnemonic_text: A bitter grass taste: nigai.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The kanji here means <kanji form="苦">suffering</kanji>, and suffering on the tongue is exactly what <vocabulary form="苦い">bitter</vocabulary> is. The い on the end marks it as a describing word.
items.reading_mnemonic: Nigel the goat gnaws lemon rind and raw dandelion stalks, pulls a long face, and calls every mouthful <reading>にがい</reading> — <reading>Nigel</reading>'s one word for <vocabulary form="苦い">bitter</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 酸（す）＋っぱい.
items.mnemonic_text: A sharp tangy bite: suppai.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The pucker that grabs both cheeks when you bite a lemon wedge by mistake is <vocabulary form="酸っぱい">sour</vocabulary>. The い ending marks it as a describing word.
items.reading_mnemonic: Dinner is a <reading>supper pie</reading> that has turned in the heat, and one forkful folds your face in half — <reading>すっぱい</reading>, the taste we call <vocabulary form="酸っぱい">sour</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: The extracted broth base: dashi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A single <reading>dash</reading> of dried fish flakes and kelp steeps in a pot of hot water. That pale infusion is <vocabulary form="だし">soup stock</vocabulary>, <reading>だし</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Mixed — 味（み）on'yomi ＋ 噌（そ）on'yomi ＋ 汁（しる）kun'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: Fermented paste (味噌) soup (汁): miso soup.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji form="味">taste</kanji> this <kanji form="噌">boisterous</kanji>, all salt and funk and noise on the tongue, comes only from fermented soybean paste stirred into a hot bowl. That bowl is <vocabulary form="味噌汁">miso soup</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 鍋（なべ）.
items.mnemonic_text: The metal (金) cooking vessel: a pot.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A heavy dish sits over a flame in the middle of the table, and everyone drops in cabbage and tofu and fishes it back out. That dish, and the shared meal made in it, is a <vocabulary form="鍋">pot / hotpot</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The <reading>neighbour</reading> hauls her huge cast-iron <reading>なべ</reading> to every winter gathering, and nobody leaves the <vocabulary form="鍋">pot / hotpot</vocabulary> hungry.

items.reading_composition: Mixed — 野（や）on'yomi ＋ 菜（さい）on'yomi ＋ 炒（いた）kun'yomi ＋ め.
items.mnemonic_text: Vegetables (野菜) fried (炒め): a stir fry.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Take <kanji form="菜">greens</kanji> pulled straight from the open <kanji form="野">field</kanji>, throw them into a scorching pan and <kanji form="炒">roast</kanji> them fast, and you have <vocabulary form="野菜炒め">stir-fried vegetables</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 寿（す）＋司（し）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: Vinegared rice with toppings: sushi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Each piece is placed with the precision of a white-gloved <kanji form="司">official</kanji>, as formal as a <kanji form="寿">congratulations</kanji> spoken aloud. That careful offering of rice and fish is <vocabulary form="寿司">sushi</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Buckwheat noodles: soba.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At the midnight stand you eat a bowl of thin grey buckwheat noodles to stay <reading>sober</reading> after drinking. Those noodles are <vocabulary form="そば">soba noodles</vocabulary>, <reading>そば</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Thick wheat noodles: udon.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The chef barks that <reading>you don't</reading> ever roll these noodles thin, and slaps out a fat white rope of dough. That thick noodle is <vocabulary form="うどん">udon noodles</vocabulary>, <reading>うどん</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Borrowed word: raamen.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The whole stadium stands and chants <reading>rah, men</reading> after the final whistle, then pours out to queue at one steaming stall. What they queue for is a bowl of <vocabulary form="ラーメン">ramen</vocabulary>, <reading>ラーメン</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Borrowed word: karee.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Every Friday <reading>Carrie</reading> ladles a thick brown spiced stew over a mound of rice for the whole house. Her Friday dish is <vocabulary form="カレー">curry</vocabulary>, <reading>カレー</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Borrowed word: sarada.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The gardener <reading>Sarah Da</reading> tips raw leaves, sliced tomato and cold cucumber into one big wooden bowl and tosses them with oil. That cold raw bowl is a <vocabulary form="サラダ">salad</vocabulary>, <reading>サラダ</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Borrowed word: sandoicchi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The picnic filling is so gritty it is like <reading>sand, which</reading> has worked its way between two thick slabs of bread. That gritty stack is a <vocabulary form="サンドイッチ">sandwich</vocabulary>, <reading>サンドイッチ</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Borrowed word: aisukuriimu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: One touch of the cold scoop on a filled tooth and you let out an <reading>I scream</reading>. The frozen sweet that caused it is <vocabulary form="アイスクリーム">ice cream</vocabulary>, <reading>アイスクリーム</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Borrowed word: keeki.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The sponge comes out of the oven the exact dull brown-green of <reading>khaki</reading> trousers, yet it is soft and sweet. That baked sweet is a <vocabulary form="ケーキ">cake</vocabulary>, <reading>ケーキ</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Borrowed word: chokoreeto.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The bar is so dense and dry that the first bite makes you <reading>choke a lot</reading> before it finally melts. That dark sweet block is <vocabulary form="チョコレート">chocolate</vocabulary>, <reading>チョコレート</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Borrowed word: juusu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: <reading>Zeus</reading> squeezes a whole storm cloud full of oranges until it rains down into one tall glass. What fills the glass is <vocabulary form="ジュース">juice</vocabulary>, <reading>ジュース</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Borrowed word: wain.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A small child at the table starts to <reading>whine</reading> the moment the adults uncork the dark red bottle and fill their glasses. That guarded grown-up drink is <reading>ワイン</reading>, the <vocabulary form="ワイン">wine</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 服（ふく）＋装（そう）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: Clothes (服) formation (装): one's outfit.
items.meaning_mnemonic: One piece of <kanji form="服">clothing</kanji> is just that one piece. The whole matching set you put on to be seen in public is your <vocabulary form="服装">attire</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 制（せい）＋服（ふく）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: Regulated (制) clothing (服): a uniform.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <kanji form="制">rule</kanji> book fixes every piece of this <kanji form="服">clothing</kanji>, down to the buttons. The one outfit you never get to choose for yourself is a <vocabulary form="制服">uniform</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Borrowed word: nekutai.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Every morning you loop a silk strip around your neck and tie it in a snug knot. That plain <reading>neck tie</reading> is a <reading>ネクタイ</reading>, a <vocabulary form="ネクタイ">necktie</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Borrowed word: sukaato.
items.meaning_mnemonic: To <reading>skirt</reading> a puddle you swing wide around its edge. Swing your hips that way as you walk and the loose cloth that flares out from your waist is a <reading>スカート</reading>, a <vocabulary form="スカート">skirt</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Borrowed word (from French): zubon.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Sit down, feed one leg in and then the other, and <reading>zip on</reading> the two cloth tubes. Fastened at your waist, that pair of tubes is <reading>ズボン</reading>, your <vocabulary form="ズボン">trousers</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Borrowed word: seetaa.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Pull the thick wool top down over your head and within a minute you start to <reading>sweat</reading>. The heavy knitted layer that does that to you is a <reading>セーター</reading>, a <vocabulary form="セーター">sweater</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 靴（くつ）＋下（した）.
items.mnemonic_text: Under (下) the shoes (靴): socks.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Hidden <kanji form="下">below</kanji> your <kanji form="靴">shoes</kanji> all day where nobody sees them, wrapped straight onto the foot, are your <vocabulary form="靴下">socks</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 手（て）＋袋（ぶくろ）. Rendaku: 袋 ふくろ → ぶくろ.
items.mnemonic_text: A bag (袋) for the hand (手): gloves.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A snug <kanji form="袋">sack</kanji> sewn to the shape of a <kanji form="手">hand</kanji>, with a separate slot for each finger, is one of a pair of <vocabulary form="手袋">gloves</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 指（ゆび）＋輪（わ）.
items.mnemonic_text: A ring (輪) for the finger (指): a ring.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A metal band sized to slide onto one <kanji form="指">finger</kanji> and stay there is a <vocabulary form="指輪">ring</vocabulary> you wear as jewelry.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Borrowed word: nekkuresu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Slip the jewelled chain off your collarbones and the bare skin leaves your <reading>neck less</reading> dressed than before. Put the chain back to fix that and you are wearing a <reading>ネックレス</reading>, a <vocabulary form="ネックレス">necklace</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Borrowed word: baggu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Load a leather shoulder <reading>bag</reading> with your purse, phone and keys until its sides go round and firm. Carried as part of an outfit, that piece is a <reading>バッグ</reading>, a <vocabulary form="バッグ">bag</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Borrowed word: saizu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The tailor runs the tape around your chest, reads the number, and <reading>sighs</reading>. That number, how big your clothes have to be, is your <reading>サイズ</reading>, your <vocabulary form="サイズ">size</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Irregular — わりびき cannot be assembled from the dictionary readings of 割引.
items.mnemonic_text: Splitting (割) and pulling (引) off the price: a discount.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Cut the price into equal <kanji form="割">proportion</kanji>s, then <kanji form="引">pull</kanji> a few of those parts away before you pay. The parts pulled off the total are the <vocabulary form="割引">discount</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Wally jabs a <reading>wobbly key</reading> into the till and springs the drawer open. He counts cash back into your hand off the price you owed, and that money handed back is a <reading>わりびき</reading>, a <vocabulary form="割引">discount</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 売（う）＋り＋場（ば）.
items.mnemonic_text: A place (場) to sell (売る): a sales counter.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The lit patch of <kanji form="場">place</kanji> on a shop floor where the staff do nothing but <kanji form="売">sell</kanji> one kind of goods is that department's <vocabulary form="売り場">sales floor</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Mixed — 支（し）on'yomi ＋ 払（はら）kun'yomi ＋ う.
items.mnemonic_text: Supporting (支) and paying (払う): to settle a bill.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Handing a shop the exact money you owe helps <kanji form="支">support</kanji> it for another day. The formal verb for passing that money across the counter is <vocabulary form="支払う">to pay</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 領（りょう）＋収（しゅう）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: Governing (領) collection (収): a formal receipt.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Once the shop has <kanji form="収">reaped</kanji> your payment into its own <kanji form="領">territory</kanji>, it hands you a slip proving the money changed hands. That slip is a <vocabulary form="領収">receipt</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 注（ちゅう）＋文（もん）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: Pouring (注) a written request (文): an order.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji form="注">pour</kanji> one clear <kanji form="文">sentence</kanji> across the counter, telling the shop exactly what you want. That sentence is your <vocabulary form="注文">order</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 交（こう）＋換（かん）＋する, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: Crossing (交) a change (換): to exchange.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Two people let their goods <kanji form="交">mingle</kanji> on the table, then <kanji form="換">change</kanji> which one each takes home. What they do is <vocabulary form="交換する">to exchange</vocabulary> them.

items.word_type: する verb, transitive verb, intransitive verb
items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 返（へん）＋品（ぴん）＋する, each kanji read with its on'yomi. Handakuon: 品 ひん → ぴん.
items.mnemonic_text: Returning (返) the goods (品): to return an item.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You carry the <kanji form="品">goods</kanji> back to the counter that sold them and hand them over for a refund. Doing that is <vocabulary form="返品する">to return an item</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 健（けん）＋康（こう）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: Strong (健) and peaceful (康): good health.
items.meaning_mnemonic: When every part of your body has settled into <kanji form="康">ease</kanji> and nothing in it aches or strains, the single word for that whole calm state is <vocabulary form="健康">health</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 体（たい）＋重（じゅう）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: The body's (体) heaviness (重): body weight.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Step on a scale and it tells you one thing: how <kanji form="重">heavy</kanji> the <kanji form="体">body</kanji> you carry around all day has become. That one number is your <vocabulary form="体重">body weight</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 身（しん）＋長（ちょう）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: The body's (身) length (長): one's height.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Stand a <kanji form="身">person</kanji> against the wall and measure how <kanji form="長">long</kanji> they are from heel to crown. That measurement is their <vocabulary form="身長">height (body)</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: On'yomi — 熱（ねつ）.
items.mnemonic_text: A hot (熱) burning inside: a fever.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Lay the back of your hand on a sick child's forehead and it comes away warm, like a pebble left out in full sun. That trapped warmth pouring off the skin is a <vocabulary form="熱">fever / heat</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 咳（せき）.
items.mnemonic_text: A mouth (口) releasing air suddenly: a cough.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A hard bark of air fires up your throat with no warning and rattles the whole quiet room. That sharp, helpless burst is a <vocabulary form="咳">cough</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi tears open a <reading>sack</reading> of flour at the konbini and breathes the white cloud straight in. It punches out a <reading>せき</reading> loud enough to stop the beeping till, because a chestful of flour always ends in a <vocabulary form="咳">cough</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Irregular — かぜをひく cannot be assembled from the dictionary readings of 風邪をひく.
items.mnemonic_text: Pulling (引く) the cold wind (風邪) in: to catch a cold.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Pull a <kanji form="邪">wicked</kanji> <kanji form="風">wind</kanji> deep into your chest and let it settle in as a three-day fever. Drawing bad air right inside you like that is what it means <vocabulary form="風邪をひく">to catch a cold</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A cold gust off the river hooks Kaz like a fish on a line and reels him straight into bed. When chilled air <reading>hooks</reading> into you and holds on, that is <reading>かぜをひく</reading>, <vocabulary form="風邪をひく">to catch a cold</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 治（ち）＋療（りょう）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: Governing (治) and healing (療): treatment.
items.meaning_mnemonic: First you get the disease to <kanji form="治">calm down</kanji>, then you <kanji form="療">heal</kanji> the damage it left behind. Doing both of those, in that order, is <vocabulary form="治療">medical treatment</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 注（ちゅう）＋射（しゃ）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: Pouring (注) a shot (射): an injection.
items.meaning_mnemonic: An <vocabulary form="注射">injection</vocabulary> is a dose <kanji form="射">shot</kanji> through a thin needle so it <kanji form="注">pours</kanji> straight into your blood instead of going down your throat.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 手（しゅ）＋術（じゅつ）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: A hand's (手) craft (術): surgery.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <vocabulary form="手術">surgery</vocabulary> is a trained <kanji form="手">hand</kanji> putting every bit of its learned <kanji form="術">technique</kanji> to work inside a body that has been opened up.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 入（にゅう）＋院（いん）＋する, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: Entering (入) the hospital (院): to be admitted.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You <kanji form="入">enter</kanji> the medical <kanji form="院">institution</kanji> as a patient, the doors fall shut, and you are not sleeping at home tonight. Ending up kept inside like that is what it means <vocabulary form="入院する">to be hospitalized</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 退（たい）＋院（いん）＋する, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: Retreating (退) from the hospital (院): to be discharged.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The morning you can finally stand on your own, you <kanji form="退">withdraw</kanji> from the <kanji form="院">institution</kanji> and walk back out to the street. Getting yourself out the doors like that is <vocabulary form="退院する">to leave hospital</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 健（けん）＋康（こう）＋診（しん）＋断（だん）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: A health (健康) diagnosis (診断): a checkup.
items.furigana: 健[けん]康[こう]診[しん]断[だん]
items.meaning_mnemonic: Once a year a doctor checks whether every part of you is running at <kanji form="康">ease</kanji>, then draws a firm <kanji form="断">severance</kanji> line between what passed and what a specialist must chase. That whole yearly review is a <vocabulary form="健康診断">health checkup</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 薬（くすり）＋を＋飲（の）＋む.
items.mnemonic_text: Drinking (飲む) the medicine (薬): to take medicine.
items.meaning_mnemonic: English says you take a pill; Japanese says you <kanji form="飲">drink</kanji> it. So even a dry tablet of <kanji form="薬">medicine</kanji> goes down the same way water does, and that is what it means <vocabulary form="薬を飲む">to take medicine</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 怪（け）＋我（が）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: A mysterious (怪) loss (我): an injury.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <kanji form="怪">mysterious</kanji> shape swings out of the dark and catches the one <kanji form="我">self</kanji> you were busy minding. Whatever it leaves on you afterward, a gash or a sprain or a spreading bruise, is an <vocabulary form="怪我">injury</vocabulary>.

items.word_type: する verb, transitive verb, intransitive verb
items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 怪（け）＋我（が）＋する, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: Suffering a mysterious loss: to be injured.
items.meaning_mnemonic: When a <kanji form="怪">suspicious</kanji> force blindsides your own <kanji form="我">self</kanji> and something tears or swells with nobody's hand on it, that event is what it means <vocabulary form="怪我する">to get injured</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 痛（いた）＋む.
items.mnemonic_text: A sickness (疒) piercing through steadily: to ache.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A back tooth starts to throb late at night with nobody near it and nothing pressing on it. When a part of you sends up that steady, unasked-for pain on its own, it has begun <vocabulary form="痛む">to hurt / ache</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already know 痛 is 「いた」 from 痛い, so for a sore knee <vocabulary form="痛む">to hurt / ache</vocabulary> on its own is <reading>いたむ</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 目（め）＋が＋悪（わる）＋い.
items.mnemonic_text: The eyes (目) being bad (悪い): poor vision.
items.meaning_mnemonic: When the <kanji form="目">eye</kanji> itself has gone <kanji form="悪">bad</kanji> and anything past your own arm is a blur, that is <vocabulary form="目が悪い">to have poor eyesight</vocabulary>. The final い is the ending that makes it an adjective.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 耳（みみ）＋が＋遠（とお）＋い.
items.mnemonic_text: The ears (耳) being far (遠い): hard of hearing.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Your <kanji form="耳">ear</kanji> still works, but every sound now has to cross a long <kanji form="遠">distant</kanji> road to reach it and arrives faint. Sound landing that far off is <vocabulary form="耳が遠い">to be hard of hearing</vocabulary>, and the closing い marks it as an adjective.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Borrowed word: supootsuman.
items.meaning_mnemonic: <reading>スポーツマン</reading> is just the English words <reading>sports man</reading> pushed together, and a man whose whole week is training and games is an <vocabulary form="スポーツマン">athlete</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 運（うん）＋動（どう）＋する, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: Carrying (運) motion (動): to exercise.
items.meaning_mnemonic: What it means <vocabulary form="運動する">to exercise</vocabulary> is to <kanji form="運">carry</kanji> your own body through enough hard <kanji form="動">motion</kanji> to leave you breathless.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 野（や）＋球（きゅう）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: Field (野) ball (球): baseball.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Take the open <kanji form="野">field</kanji> the village never fenced, add one hard <kanji form="球">ball</kanji> and nine leather gloves, and the game they play out there is <vocabulary form="野球">baseball</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Borrowed word: sakkaa.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A striker drops one shoulder and the goalkeeper lunges the wrong way like a <reading>sucker</reading>. Ninety minutes of fooling the last defender like that is <vocabulary form="サッカー">soccer</vocabulary>, <reading>サッカー</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Borrowed word: basukettobooru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A street <reading>busker</reading> gives up on coins. He nails his hat to a lamppost, lobs a rubber ball through it again and again, and that hooped, hand-thrown game is <vocabulary form="バスケットボール">basketball</vocabulary>, <reading>バスケットボール</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Borrowed word: tenisu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Two <reading>tenants</reading> on either side of a net argue over every bounce by whacking a ball back across it. That racket-swung quarrel is <vocabulary form="テニス">tennis</vocabulary>, <reading>テニス</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Borrowed word: gorufu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A ball sails off the tee, clears a wide sandy <reading>gulf</reading> of a bunker, and drops beside a little flag. Walking eighteen of those crossings in an afternoon is <vocabulary form="ゴルフ">golf</vocabulary>, <reading>ゴルフ</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 水（すい）＋泳（えい）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: Water (水) swimming (泳): swimming.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A lane of nothing but <kanji form="水">water</kanji>, and you crossing it end to end under your own power with just arms and legs, is what <vocabulary form="水泳">swimming</vocabulary> is.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Borrowed word: sukii.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Strap two long boards to your boots, point the tips downhill, and let them run over the snow with a <reading>squeaky</reading> hiss all the way to the bottom. That boarded slide is <vocabulary form="スキー">skiing</vocabulary>, <reading>スキー</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Borrowed word: dansu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <reading>dunce</reading> sent to stand in the corner gets bored and starts swaying, then spinning, then throwing shapes to music only he can hear. Moving your body in time like that is <vocabulary form="ダンス">dance</vocabulary>, <reading>ダンス</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 楽（がっ）＋器（き）, each kanji read with its on'yomi. Gemination: 楽 がく → がっ.
items.mnemonic_text: A music (楽) tool (器): an instrument.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Take a hollow <kanji form="器">vessel</kanji>, a stretched drum or a boxed rack of strings, and build it so that striking it gives off <kanji form="楽">music</kanji>. Any container made for that is a <vocabulary form="楽器">musical instrument</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Borrowed word: piano.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A concert announcer rolls the name of the big lacquered keyboard out slow and grand, <reading>pee-AH-no</reading>, and the lid lifts back off eighty-eight keys. That strung box of felt hammers is a <vocabulary form="ピアノ">piano</vocabulary>, <reading>ピアノ</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Borrowed word: gitaa.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The six strings stretched over the flat wooden box are so sticky they might as well be strung with <reading>gee, tar</reading>, yet you still strum them for a tune. That sticky-stringed box is a <vocabulary form="ギター">guitar</vocabulary>, <reading>ギター</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Mixed — 将（しょう）on'yomi ＋ 来（らい）on'yomi ＋ の ＋ 夢（ゆめ）kun'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: A future's (将来) dream (夢): one's aspiration.
items.furigana: 将[しょう]来[らい]の夢[ゆめ]
items.meaning_mnemonic: The plan a <kanji form="将">general</kanji> lays out for the battles still to <kanji form="来">come</kanji>, years before any of it starts, is what an ordinary person calls a <vocabulary form="将来の夢">future dream</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 読（どく）＋書（しょ）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: Reading (読) books (書): reading as a hobby.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Sitting down with pages someone else took the trouble to <kanji form="書">write</kanji>, and working through them line by line to <kanji form="読">read</kanji> them, is <vocabulary form="読書">reading (books)</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 小（しょう）＋説（せつ）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: A small (小) telling (説): a novel.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Take one writer's <kanji form="小">small</kanji>, made-up <kanji form="説">explanation</kanji> of how some invented life might go, then stretch it across three hundred pages. That padded little theory is a <vocabulary form="小説">novel</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 漫（まん）＋画（が）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: Loose (漫) drawings (画): manga.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Draw one loose, <kanji form="漫">unrestrained</kanji> <kanji form="画">picture</kanji>, then the next, then a hundred more in a row, and bind the stack. That runaway sequence of drawings is <vocabulary form="漫画">comic / manga</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Borrowed word: geemu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Kids too broke for a real board split one stick of <reading>gum</reading> as the prize and make up rules for winning it on the spot. Any contest run like that is a <vocabulary form="ゲーム">game</vocabulary>, <reading>ゲーム</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kun'yomi — 釣（つ）＋り.
items.mnemonic_text: Hooking (釣る) a catch: fishing.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Sit on the riverbank, bait a hook, and drop it on a long line into the water. Waiting like that for something below to pull is <vocabulary form="釣り">fishing</vocabulary>.
items.reading_mnemonic: You already met this sound as 「つ」 in お釣り, the change handed back at a shop, so the word for <vocabulary form="釣り">fishing</vocabulary> is just <reading>つり</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Borrowed word: toranpu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: In a game of whist the one suit that beats all the others is the <reading>trump</reading>, and the full deck you deal it from is <vocabulary form="トランプ">playing cards</vocabulary>, <reading>トランプ</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 将（しょう）＋棋（ぎ）, each kanji read with its on'yomi. Rendaku: 棋 き → ぎ.
items.mnemonic_text: A general's (将) board game (棋): shogi.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A board game where you push wooden <kanji form="将">commander</kanji>s and their foot soldiers across a grid, hunting the enemy leader until he has no move left, is <vocabulary form="将棋">shogi (chess)</vocabulary>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Borrowed word: konpyuutaa.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A grey desk machine that grinds through a million sums a second is a thing that <reading>computes</reading>, and the flat everyday name for it is <vocabulary form="コンピューター">computer</vocabulary>, <reading>コンピューター</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Borrowed word: intaanetto.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You <reading>enter a net</reading> stretched over the whole planet, and every fact anyone ever wrote hangs caught in its mesh, in reach from wherever you stand. That worldwide catch is the <vocabulary form="インターネット">internet</vocabulary>, and its name is the sound of stepping in: <reading>インターネット</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Borrowed word: meeru.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You post a paper letter through a slot and it thumps onto a desk across the planet before the flap has swung back. <reading>Mail</reading> that fast is <vocabulary form="メール">email</vocabulary>, and the slot clacks out <reading>メール</reading> every time one lands.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Borrowed word: saito.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You tap in an address and a whole shop unfolds where your blank screen was, shelves and counter and a visitor book by the door. A <reading>sight</reading> you can step into like that is a <vocabulary form="サイト">website</vocabulary>, and it goes by <reading>サイト</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Borrowed word: apuri.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You press one bright square on the glass and it does exactly one job — counts your steps, nothing else. A small program you <reading>apply</reading> to a single task is an <vocabulary form="アプリ">app</vocabulary>, and every square on that screen is one <reading>アプリ</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 伝（でん）＋言（ごん）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: Passed (伝) words (言): a message.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <vocabulary form="伝言">message (spoken)</vocabulary> is a run of <kanji form="言">words</kanji> you hand to one person so they can <kanji form="伝">carry it along</kanji> to the next, mouth to mouth, with nothing written down.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 連（れん）＋絡（らく）＋する, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: Connecting (連) a network (絡): to get in touch.
items.meaning_mnemonic: To <vocabulary form="連絡する">contact</vocabulary> someone is to <kanji form="連">join</kanji> your thread to theirs and <kanji form="絡">coil</kanji> the two ends together, so a tug you give is felt at their end.

items.reading_composition: Jukugo — 画（が）＋面（めん）, each kanji read with its on'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: A drawn (画) face (面): a screen.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <vocabulary form="画面">screen (display)</vocabulary> is the flat <kanji form="面">face</kanji> of the device, and every <kanji form="画">picture</kanji> it shows is painted straight onto that face.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Borrowed word: sofuto.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The metal box on your desk is the hard part of the machine; the <reading>soft</reading> part is the lists of instructions inside, which you can rewrite without turning a single screw. That rewritable half is <vocabulary form="ソフト">software</vocabulary>, and you call it <reading>ソフト</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Digital camera, shortened: dejikame.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You point it, press once, and the shot is already a grid of numbers on a card — no film, no developing tray. A <reading>digi-cam</reading> that keeps every picture as bare digits is a <vocabulary form="デジカメ">digital camera</vocabulary>, and its name is <reading>デジカメ</reading>.

items.reading_composition: Mixed — 番（ばん）on'yomi ＋ 組（ぐみ）kun'yomi.
items.mnemonic_text: A numbered (番) set (組): a program.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <vocabulary form="番組">TV program</vocabulary> is a single <kanji form="番">numbered turn</kanji> in the evening's run, <kanji form="組">braided</kanji> between the show before it and the show after so the night plays with no gap.

items.reading_composition: Kana only — the word is written exactly as it is read.
items.mnemonic_text: Borrowed word: nyuusu.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The bundle on the counter holds nothing but <reading>new</reading> things — a fire last night, a price that jumped this morning, none of it old yet.
